newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine gov't pushes for pay deals by company.
newsitem.headline: Argentine gov't pushes for pay deals by company.

text.p: The Argentine government is pushing for pay negotiations by firm rather than by industry in proposed new labor laws aimed at loosening up what it calls excessive centralization and rigidity in the current system.
President Carlos Menem's Peronist government released details late Wednesday of its proposed bill on collective pay deals -- a key chapter of its campaign for more flexible labor legislation.
Menem argues that more modern labor laws are the solution to Argentina's current 17.1 unemployment.
- pay negotiation by company rather than by industry.
- allowing companies to pay the mandatory twice-yearly "aguinaldo" bonuses in up to three quotas.
- 12 special labor regimes such as those for journalists, bank workers and commercial travelers being scrapped.
The text of the proposed bill insists that pay deals will be fixed-term "and not considered as acquired rights."
Caro Figueroa denied newspaper reports that the bill also allowed for firms to demand employees work 30 consecutive days with weekends worked taken as leave at the end of the month.

The project, in which Menem also wants to swap termination payouts for unemployment insurance and make wages partly variable depending on the economic climate, is fiercely opposed by trade unions, who have staged two general strikes in two months.

Labor Minister Armando Caro Figueroa told local radio that the pay negotiation proposal "means not just decentralization and modernization of working conditions but also the need for unions to decentralize their own structure."
The government-sponsored pay negotiation bill, which has yet to be sent to Congress, would establish:
"The project does foresee some modifications in working hours and time off, but this must always be subject to the collective negotiation," said the minister.
An opinion poll published in La Nacion newspaper Thursday showed that 53 percent favored going even further and holding wage negotiations between each employee and his company.

Just 14 percent favored pay deals being struck between the union and business sector and 6.0 percent between unions and each company. Eight percent were in favor of wage negotiation between union representatives and management in each company.
The survey by pollsters Manuel Mora y Araujo in Buenos Aires and surrounding districts was carried out in May and June -- just before Menem launched his labor law campaign.
It showed that while 42 percent believed pay should be the same for all workers in the same category, 48 percent believed pay should vary depending on each individual's performance.
